fixes.where: Faith as obedient trust, John 3:36 note
readers: a secular academic scholar of religion
fixes.why: The current note says the Greek word 'is glossed not obeying, which sets believing and obeying side by side.' The gloss is real (apeithon, 'not obeying', in the site's word-by-word data), but the sentence gives only one side of a live lexical question. The verb apeitheo covers both refusing to believe and refusing to obey, and the verse sets it against 'believes', so many scholars and the Berean (which renders 'rejects') read it as unbelief. A reader who does not hold this reading would see the note as arguing for it, and the sentence reads as the site's finding rather than as what holders of the reading take from it. The other readings could also cite the verse (the first sentence, 'whoever believes ... has eternal life', is a standard text for faith alone).
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: "The Greek word the Berean renders “rejects” (apeithōn) can mean refusing to believe or refusing to obey, and the site’s word-by-word gloss is “not obeying”. Holders of this reading take it as setting believing and obeying side by side; others take it as the opposite of believing, and cite the verse’s first sentence for life given to the one who believes." Optionally add to the faith-alone reading's 'answers': "They take John 3:36 to set belief against refusal to believe, and to promise life to the one who believes."

readers: a secular academic scholar of religion
fixes.why: 'Quotes Genesis 15:6: righteousness credited in response to belief' states Paul's reading of the Hebrew verse as the verse's own meaning. The Hebrew (wayyaḥšəbeha lo ṣədaqah, 'and he reckoned it to him as righteousness') does not name who does the reckoning, and the Berean's Genesis text says only 'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness'. Genesis 15:6 on its own does not decide the later Christian debate, and the note must say whose reading it is.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: "Quotes Genesis 15:6 (“Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”). Holders of this reading take Paul to show there that righteousness was credited to Abraham for believing, before any work."

fixes.where: terms (new entry) and the faith-alone and faith-working-through-love 'answers'
readers: a secular academic scholar of religion
fixes.why: On the editor's question: Genesis 15:6 does need a place, but not as a ninth passage in one reading (that would unbalance the counts and file a Hebrew verse under a Christian position). Paul (Rom 4:3) and James (Jas 2:23) both cite it, so it is common ground that the debate turns on, and the readings differ over what it shows. Its Jewish reading is also different again: Abraham's faith is trust (emunah) and is read together with Genesis 22:12 and 26:5, where obedience is named. A rabbi would object to Genesis 15:6 appearing only through Paul. Literary readers of Genesis would add that Abraham's belief (15:6) and the test of Genesis 22 are the two ends of one arc, which both Paul and James use. Without a place of its own the card shows the verse only in the first reading's rival's hands.
fixes.fix: Add a term entry: {"term": "Abraham and Genesis 15:6", "note": "Paul (Romans 4:3) and James (James 2:23) both quote Genesis 15:6, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” The readings differ over what it shows: that righteousness is credited for believing before any work, or a faith that Abraham’s later obedience brought to completion (James 2:22). Jewish readers take Abraham’s belief as trust in God and read it with Genesis 22:12, “now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me”, and Genesis 26:5, “because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.” Where the Hebrew says “it was credited to him”, it does not name who credited it."} Also add "Genesis 15:6" to related.passages if the schema allows, or leave it in the term. The rabbi seat should confirm the Jewish-readers sentence.

fixes.why: James 2:21-23 is the argument that this reading and the faith-alone reading both turn on, and the card cites James 2:22 in this reading but never shows verse 23, which is the link back to Genesis 15:6 that makes the dispute readable. It is cited in the faith-alone answers, but a reader sees only its address.
fixes.fix: Swap 1 Corinthians 15:10 or Philippians 2:12 for James 2:23 with quote "And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God." and note "Quotes Genesis 15:6 and names Abraham’s works with it (James 2:21-22): read as faith and deeds belonging together." Keep 8 per reading. If the editor prefers to keep Philippians 2:12-13 as a pair, drop 1 Corinthians 15:10.

readers: a secular academic scholar of religion
fixes.why: The term is fair, but the three senses carry no attribution, and the third (practices that marked Jewish identity) is a recent scholarly proposal that some Christian traditions reject. Left unattributed, it reads as the site's own view of the scholarship.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: "Paul’s phrase in Romans 3:28 and Galatians 2:16. Traditions and scholars differ over whether it means good works in general, the Mosaic law as a whole, or the practices that marked Jewish identity (the last often called the New Perspective on Paul); each sense is held by some Christian readers and some scholars."

summary: Every quote is the Berean's exact words and the three readings are stated fairly, with balanced counts, in their holders' own terms and with no verdict I could find. Two things need fixing before it ships: the John 3:36 note presents one side of a lexical question as the verse's meaning, and Genesis 15:6 needs a place of its own as a verse both Paul and James cite and the Jewish tradition reads differently, with the Romans 4:3 note reworded so the Christian reading of it is attributed.
